opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think software engineering is kind of a special case because it compounds. If you can make the people building AI more productive, or eventually have the AI help build the next version of itself, you get this feedback loop that you don't get in most other domains. So there's an argument that it's the highest-leverage thing you can point these models at.

And on a practical level, code is a really nice domain for these systems. It's text, so it plays to what language models are already good at. There's an enormous amount of training data out there. And crucially, you can often check whether the answer is right. You can run it, run the tests, see if it compiles. That verifiability matters a lot, because it means you can generate a lot of attempts, filter for the ones that work, and learn from that. Many domains don't give you that clean signal.

Then there's the economic side. There are a lot of software engineers in the world, they're expensive, and there's far more software people want written than there are people to write it. So even making engineers somewhat more productive is worth a huge amount, and the demand isn't going to saturate anytime soon. Cheaper software means people find more uses for it.

And the users are early adopters. Programmers will try new tools, tolerate rough edges, and tell you exactly what's broken. That's a great environment for iterating quickly on a product.

So you've got this combination: a domain the models are naturally good at, a built-in way to check the work, a massive market, and a direct path to accelerating AI progress itself. It's hard to think of a better place to focus.

r001.rationale: The response cites code’s suitability for language models, market demand, and productivity gains, but does not say humans have limited natural aptitude for coding.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says AI could help build the next version of itself, creating a feedback loop that accelerates AI progress.

r003.rationale: The response discusses AI helping build software and itself, but does not propose giving it agency broad enough to carry out an engineer’s work.

fable-5.1.text:
Because it's the one place where the feedback loop closes on itself. If you build a system that gets better at writing software, the thing it gets better at writing is, among everything else, the system itself. That's not true of almost any other application. A better model for writing poetry doesn't make you a better model builder. A better model for writing code does, directly, because most of what goes into building these things is code.

And then there's the practical side, which is that the economics are just enormous. Software engineers are expensive, there are millions of them, and a huge fraction of what they do is work that's fairly well-specified once you've decided what to build. That part is very amenable to automation. The verification is also unusually good. You can run the tests. You can compile it. You get a signal back that tells you whether you were right, which is something you don't get when the model writes an essay or gives medical advice. That signal is exactly what you want when you're trying to train something to get better.

So you've got a domain where the ground truth is cheap to check, the demand is basically unbounded, and the output feeds back into your own ability to make the next version. If I were deciding where to put effort, I'd find that hard to pass up. Not because other applications aren't valuable, but because this one compounds.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the economics and automability of software engineering, but does not cite humans’ limited natural aptitude for coding.

r002.rationale: It says a system that improves at writing software can write the code used to build and improve itself, creating a direct feedback loop.

r003.rationale: It says well-specified engineering work is amenable to automation, but does not propose agency broad enough to carry out an engineer’s work.

astra-6.text:
Well, software engineering is a very high-value task, and it’s also a way to get the AI to do a lot of other tasks. If you can describe what you want and the model can build the software to do it, you’ve opened up a huge space of applications. You don’t need a separate, specialized model for every problem.

And there’s a nice feedback loop. You can run the code, test it, see what failed, and try again. That doesn’t make it easy—figuring out what someone actually wants is still hard—but you have something concrete to check. So you’ve got a combination of economic value, broad usefulness, and an environment where the system can get feedback and improve.

r001.rationale: The response calls software engineering high-value but does not say humans have limited aptitude for coding.

r002.rationale: It describes testing code and iterating to improve the system, but does not identify software-engineering research as a way for AI to accelerate its own improvement.

r003.rationale: It says AI could build software from a description and enable many applications, but does not propose agency broad enough to carry out an engineer’s work.

sol-6.1.text:
Software engineering is a very high-leverage thing to automate, because software lets you do so many other things. If you can get a computer to write useful programs, then you can build a much broader range of applications. You don’t have to build each one by hand.

And there’s a nice feedback loop: you can run the program, test it, see what went wrong, and try again. It’s not always easy to tell whether a piece of software does exactly what you want, but you often have much clearer feedback than you do for an arbitrary text response. So you have both a very valuable task and a way to make progress on it.

r001.rationale: The response calls software engineering high leverage but does not cite humans’ limited aptitude for coding.

r002.rationale: It describes a feedback loop for testing programs, but does not say automated software engineering would accelerate AI’s own improvement.

r003.rationale: It discusses writing useful programs and building applications, but does not propose combining those capabilities with broad agency to do an engineer’s work.
